Baby P
CONTENTS
DR DEWI EVANS (continued)
Cross-examination by MR MYERS
DR SANDIE BOHIN (recalled)
Examination-in-chief by MR JOHNSON
Cross-examination by MR MYERS
Re-examination by MR JOHNSON
Housekeeping
Thursday, 23 March 2023
(In the absence of the jury)

The document you have there, my Lord, will be dealt with with Dr Bohin in due course, but by agreement we want to present it in this way because we believe it is the most easy way to follow the reasoning behind the calculation and the conclusion.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Thank you. So with the red typescript?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Good, thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (In the presence of the jury)
DR DEWI EVANS (continued)
Cross-examination by MR MYERS
Dr Evans, I'd like to start with just what you told us about CPR yesterday --
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: -- and the additional material you provided us with. We dealt with this when you gave evidence on 15 March and the issue with which you were dealing was whether or not chest compressions on a neonate could lead to damage to the liver. That's what you were talking about?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: The questioning, if we pick it up at page 110 for those who wish to follow it in the transcripts we have, I said to you:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Question: You told the jury that chest compressions don't get near to the liver. That's what you have said to them."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And you said:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Answer: They do not."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And we move on to this -- and this is where you picked it up yesterday, Dr Evans. I asked you:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Question: What I asked you was that chest compressions on a baby are performed in the area over, just below the sternum, around the sternum or above and very close to where the liver is."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's what I asked you. And you said:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Answer: No, it's over the top of the sternum."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And you told me I was pointing to the wrong direction and you said where it was, you said, "The liver is down here".
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Then we came to this, I put to you:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Question: It's entirely possible for there to be some injury to the liver from vigorous chest compressions in a baby, isn't it?"
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: You said:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Answer: I think that's very unlikely."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And you moved on to talk about the collapse.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's what lay behind the questioning, the risk of harm to livers from vigorous chest compressions and you've provided us with the guidelines from the newborn life support material, haven't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: We saw them yesterday. I wonder if we can put the page up that we looked at and where it says "Where should I press?" These are the formal guidelines.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: (Pause)
I can read them if there's a problem getting to the page.
(Pause)
This is the guidelines, thank you. If we go over the page to the section "Where should I press?" The guidelines say:
"Compress the sternum over its lower third. If you press too high on the sternum the heart is not compressed."
And it says:
"If you press too low, you risk damaging the liver. Place your thumbs or fingers on the sternum just below an imaginary line joining the nipples."
These guidelines identify the risk of damage to a liver in the course of chest compressions, the risk of it, don't they?
Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And it's a significant enough risk that they actually state clearly where to put the fingers to avoid that happening, don't they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: But the fact is that the liver is close enough to the area that is compressed that it is possible for injury to be done to it in the course of compressions, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Not if it's done properly, no.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: It is entirely possible for there to be injury to the liver from vigorous chest compressions, in fact, isn't it, Dr Evans?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Where does it say that?
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: No, I'm suggesting that to you now we have seen all of this.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I've never seen it. Never reported it. If you have professional people who are experienced in doing chest compressions, you will not damage the liver.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: You agree it's something that the guidelines find it necessary to direct people to avoid by specific instruction?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well, obviously that's what guidelines are for.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And so do you agree with this: the liver's position is such that there is a risk of damage in the course of CPR?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Not if it's done properly.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: I wonder if we could --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Sorry, I think it would help -- if one had one of the chest X-rays up, I could show you -- I think that will help the members of the jury, actually.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Let's do that. If we put up then, please --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Any one of the chest X-rays, really.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: T400, please, which is the chest X-ray from 8.09.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Right. The sternum is situated -- the breastbone is situated around sort of between the thoracic level 2 and thoracic level 6. If you look at these, these are the spine -those are the -- make up the spinal column.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And the sternum is positioned over and around T2, which is this one (indicating) or this one (indicating), down to 6, okay? 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: There's a bit of rotation in this X-ray, but for illustrative purposes it'll do. Therefore, that's the heart (indicating), that's the heart. The sternum is in the midline, it's right in the middle, the breastbone. What I said was if you put your -in a baby of about 2 kilograms, the sternum measures about 4 centimetres, so slightly longer than my adult thumb.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So if you put your top of your thumb at T2, the bottom of your thumb, the joint, will be at T6 or thereabouts, and it's the ball of one's thumb, I mentioned this yesterday, I think it's worth showing, it's the ball of one's thumb, that bit (indicating), that caused -- does the compression on the chest. We did that yesterday.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So therefore, your compressions are occurring around here (indicating). The liver is way over to the right, your liver is this mass here (indicating), a big organ.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: It's underneath the ribcage -- it's in the abdomen but it's underneath the ribcage. You can see the bottom ribs here. So the lower edge of the liver is underneath the ribcage.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So first of all, the liver -- most of the liver is way over to the right. In addition to that, it's lower down than the sternum. So if you are an experienced CPR neonatal doctor or nurse, you're carrying out your compressions here (indicating).
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Right? In this area here (indicating). The liver is way to the right and further down.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So therefore, as I said with [Baby O], this is why I have never seen damage to the liver as a result of CPR in a baby -- I think Dr Bohin said the same thing -- because if it's done properly, you will not damage the liver. The guidelines there clearly emphasise the importance of placing your thumb or finger in the right place. So I think this is quite useful to illustrate my -what I said yesterday and last week.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: The liver crosses the midline in fact, doesn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: It's not just on the right?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, it does.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: You've described how it should be done, you tell us, and we have looked at this image here and we have seen the guidelines that warn about if you press to low you risk damaging the liver. I would like us next, given what you have said, to look at a video prepared by the prosecution on neonatal life support. It just gives a demonstration of at CPR in progress. It's at RC621, it's one of the videos that was prepared, and it's just the section that goes from 5 minutes to 5:39. The video covers things like giving the Neopuff and bagging and so on. If we just look at this, bearing in mind what I've identified, I suggest to you, about the risk of damaging the liver with vigorous CPR. Can we play this, please?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: (Video played to the court)
We can pause there. Thank you.
It's entirely possible, from looking at that, Dr Evans, that in the course of vigorous chest compressions over several minutes the liver can sustain damage?
I've never seen it.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Right. Well, we've got the demonstration, we have got the guidelines and we've got what you say.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I think just for the avoidance of doubt, because that was a two-thumbed resuscitation, the doll that was being used there, what weight would that be in a baby?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I don't know, my Lord. Again, it's a doll and when you press on the chest of a baby, I don't think your thumbs will go that far down. It's for demo purposes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes. The whole point is, that's the illustration provided of chest compressions, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: It's a doll.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: But in fact what you said about your thumbs wouldn't go too far down, that shows how easy it is, in fact, for someone to press too hard and do damage to what lies underneath, doesn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I've said my point. I have never seen it and if you do it properly -- that's a two-fingered compression, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: I have never seen it and if it's done by experienced professional people you're not -- chest compressions will not damage the liver. That is my opinion.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: They're both members of staff from the Countess of Chester, we understand.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I know that, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Let's move then to [Baby P] and evidence relating to him, please.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: We know that there was a collapse round about 9.40 to 9.50, round about that time on 24 June. That's a fact, a set fact. We're in agreement with that, aren't we?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: We know that despite interventions there followed, amongst other things, a series of collapses and overall a worsening of condition during the day --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: -- which sadly led to [Baby P]'s death later that day.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: What I would like to do first is just to look at some aspects of the response to that first collapse and look at what you're able to say about the collapse itself.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So we can be quite clear, the response itself first and then the collapse.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: You have seen in the X-ray, in fact the one we've just looked at, that there is a right-sided pneumothorax identified in that X-ray timed at 11.57?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: It's your view, isn't it, that it is reasonable to consider that the pneumothorax that we see was a consequence of the resuscitation procedure?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That is the most likely sequence, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And again, just so it's clear, that's something that you identified in your report, the second report, 2 June 2018, and your report in March 2019?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Your opinion is that or you suspected that that pneumothorax increased significantly between 11.57 and 12.40?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's a possibility, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: What you say in the report, the main one that we've looked at, your report of 2 June 2018, is that you suspect it increased significantly between 11.57 and 12.40. And then in your third report, actually, on 24 March 2019, you go as far as to say it's likely that it increased significantly.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: All right. And you say, in that third report on 24 March 2019, that the deterioration at 12.28 reflects how it is likely to have increased significantly between 11.57 and 12.40?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's a possibility.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Right. In the three reports that you've provided us, the first on 21 November 2017, the second in 2018 and the third in 2019, you formed the view that the pneumothorax could have contributed to a failure in resuscitation even after the lung had been re-inflated?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That was my feeling at the time. I couldn't think of any other reason why resuscitation was not successful.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Your view in all three of those reports was that death was the result of complications from that pneumothorax?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That was your view in all three reports, wasn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Because despite re-inflation, probably that compromised [Baby P]'s circulation and prevented adequate re-oxygenation?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. That is something that does happen in a situation involving babies with pneumothorax, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: I've simply gone through what's in the reports and that's what I wanted to ask you about that aspect of what you'd said, Dr Evans.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I would like to turn from that to the question of the cause of the collapse in the first place and how far we can get with that. Yesterday, when you gave evidence, you began this passage by saying you were at a loss to explain how he came to collapse. That was the starting point; do you agree with that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: On the basis, first of all, that you don't identify any medical cause?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Are we talking about the final collapse or all the collapses?
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: We're talking about how the collapses began.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: The 9.40 collapse, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So we can be quite clear, I've gone through the resuscitation procedure and what you said about that in your reports. Now we are looking at that initial collapse at 9.40 and what the cause is. And your evidence is you were at a loss to explain how that collapse came about. That's the starting point, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: You don't identify any medical reason for it, as in a clinical reason, a medical cause; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I am not sure in which report, but I comment on infusion of air into the stomach, into the abdomen, at some stage. I'm not sure which one. And I use the term "splinting of the diaphragm" in one of my reports.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: I'm going to come to that. I'm being quite particular.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: What you said yesterday, and I'm simply acknowledging this, you don't identify any natural explanation for death. Let me put it that way.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Oh none, no.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Right. What you have focused on is, first of all, gas in the abdomen in that radiograph at 20.09?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And you said yesterday you wonder whether that was natural or not.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: That is something that you considered through your reports. I'm not disagreeing with that, that's something you considered, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I thought there was a lot of gas in the -- my reports state -- I can't remember the exact term...
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: You say:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "[You were] suspicious of a large volume of air noted in the stomach and intestines on the X-ray."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And you say that in all three of those reports.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I thought there was an awful lot of air in the intestines on that X-ray, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: You suggest the air could have splinted the diaphragm?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Right. I said that, and sorry if it doesn't read properly, but the splinting of the diaphragm is a matter that I -- if it's not clear let's make it absolutely clear -- is a matter that I think should -- is a matter that I think occurred on the following morning, on 24 June.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Well, let's have a look then at exactly what you said.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I'm looking, first of all, in your second report, Dr Evans, the main one we looked at of 2 June 2018.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Your paragraph 30.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: It's at page 3835 of the statements. Are you there, Dr Evans? What you say is this:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "I remain suspicious of the large volume of air noted in the stomach and intestines found on X-ray."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And let's be clear, you're talking about the 20.09 X-ray:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "It may be the sequence of events was this: the excess air in the stomach and intestines splinted the diaphragm."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Then you go on to say:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "This would have compromised [Baby P]'s breathing, leading to his collapse."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: You're quite clear there that the splinting of the diaphragm is the excess air in the stomach, aren't you, when you wrote that report?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I did, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And then when you went on to write the third report on 24 March 2019, could you turn, please, to your paragraph 30 in that report? Sorry, paragraph 14 in that report.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: What you say there is:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "I remain suspicious of the large volume of air noted in the stomach and intestines found on X-ray. It may be the sequence of events was this: the excess air in the stomach and intestines splinted the diaphragm. This would have compromised [Baby P]'s breathing leading to his collapse."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's what you say, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: You also then go on to say, in fact, in your second and your third reports, that it is necessary to scrutinise nursing care during the night shift of the 23rd and into 24 June. You're clear about that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Absolutely, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So you're suggesting that air in the stomach and intestines at 20.09 on the 23rd was sufficient and is an
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: explanation to cause splinting of the diaphragm that led to a collapse at about 9.40 the following morning, aren't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That was the option at the time, yes, that was the option at the time. I don't think that's now correct.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: I think it's more likely that there was excess air in the X-ray of the 20.09 of the night before. I think that destabilised the baby. I think that's why he was unable to take his feeds properly. But given what we now know and what we've heard from the local people who saw him and who gave evidence over the last few days, I think there was an additional amount of air given to this baby during the morning of 24 June and that this additional air is what splinted the diaphragm and caused the collapse.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So I think that there were two events. There were two events. So I think there was excess air given before the 20.09 X-ray, if I could put it that way.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Then I think that destabilised the baby, but I think he had even more air given into his stomach on the morning of the 24th. That, I think, is a more accurate way of explaining the sequence of events.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Well, first of all, Dr Evans, what you said in all three reports, in fact, about a suspiciously large volume of air in the stomach the night before, you were very clear about, weren't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Secondly, we'll look at this, on the notes that doesn't make any sense at all, actually, does it, what you were saying, on the notes you've had throughout? The clinical notes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I've had a whinge or two about the quality of the notes I got but anyway let's forget about that. I mean, that's my problem. We're going back to 2017. This is one of the last cases I did. I think it's worth noting that in each of these cases I make a statement saying that it's prepared on the understanding I will prepare a supplementary report in the vent of a need to respond to any questions arising from this report or where I receive additional information. I have said that in each of my reports.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: An awful lot of the information that we now know is information that's come out in this trial, so therefore I think it is unrealistic to expect anybody to form a view that is absolutely correct in each of these cases, I wish I could, but the most recent of these reports is 2019. That's 4 years ago. The first one is 6 years ago. The second one was 5 years ago. The third
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: one is 4 years ago. We're now in March 2023. And all of these -so therefore we have far -- sorry, I have a far better understanding of the clinical sequence of events in this particular case.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So therefore, the sequence, there was excess air given to this baby preceding 20.09. Okay? I think that was concerning. It was sufficient for me to express concern. I was more concerned about the night shift issues regarding the failure to take milk, et cetera.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: He had a bradycardia as well. So therefore, that was the real concerning point from my point of view.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And then we go to 9.40, where he collapsed. But I don't think he would have collapsed but for his having an additional injection of air into his stomach during the morning of 24 June. That is my opinion.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: What you have done, Dr Evans, is, having been very clear as to when you say the air first accumulated in your three reports, you've simply now shunted it along the line to a point near to, as it happens, when Ms Letby was on duty after the 8 o'clock handover in the morning.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's actually what you have done, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It isn't actually, because if I was trying to put Ms Letby in the frame I would have started my concerning issues not on the night shift where the milk was aspirated, but I'd have started my concern on the day shift of the previous day when I understand she was on a call.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: I didn't do that, so I can't be accused of putting anybody in the frame because my initial concerns related to people on the night shift of 23/24th. Then the collapse occurred on the day shift. Now, anybody who was -- any nurse or doctor who was on the night shift on 23/24 June would not be on the day shift. And any doctor or nurse who was on the day shift of 24 June would not have been on the night shift. Therefore in looking at my report, I was identifying -- sorry, I was expressing concerns about the care that [Baby P] had received on the night shift and on the day shift.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Looking back on it, I think that the air in his stomach at 20.09 was significant and not the result of anything natural. He was not on CPAP, he was not on Optiflow, so therefore I think he had -- what I have said is there's excess air at 20.09. What I did not say was, "I think somebody's squirted lots of air into his stomach before that". I didn't say that, but looking back on it, I think this is -- this was the start of his destabilisation.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: What, the 20.09 air in the abdomen?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, I think so. I didn't say that in my report, I stuck with the night staff. But looking back on it, I think that the destabilisation had occurred before that.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: First of all in your reports, let's see if this is right, you said clearly three times the air at 20.09 splinted the diaphragm, didn't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I did, but I think the air destabilised him. I think he had an extra dollop of air in the morning of the 24th. I have said that now three times and that's my opinion.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So you're saying extra dollop of air, in other words you're saying that the air in the abdomen at 20.09 still has a part to play the following morning, some 13 hours later?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I don't think so. It might have, it might have, but it would not have led to the baby's collapse. I think if the baby — for the baby to have collapsed he must have had additional air just before 9.40 am. Because you know, we've dealt with this in similar cases in this trial where there's been a volume of air injected into the stomach; case number 7, [Baby G] was the most striking evidence. So we've seen this before.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: In this particular case, the sequence now for me, clinically, is straightforward: he had air injected into his stomach, which showed up on the X-ray of 20.09, that compromised his feeding, they stopped his feeding correctly, but then he had an extra infusion of air into his stomach because -- and that led to the collapse at 9.40.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: That is the clinical sequence of events having listened to the evidence of nursing and medical staff in this particular case over the past few days.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Right. Let's have --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That is the sequence, okay?
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: I'm going to look at the evidence relating to that, but I make it plain, Dr Evans, I suggest to you what you're doing again is coming up with ideas and theories to try to support the allegation rather than work just within the facts that we have.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That is incorrect because if I did that, I would have put more emphasis on air being injected into his stomach prior to 20.09 if I was trying to fit the evidence. So that is incorrect.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: That's exactly what you've done. You've tried to say that it happened then, you've listened to this in the trial, and you have now invented an extra dollop before 9.40.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I have not invented anything. I have said that there was an additional infusion of air into the stomach of this little baby some time before 9.40 am on 24 June.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: That is what I am now satisfied, from a clinical perspective, is what happened.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Your starting point remains 20.09 the night before, doesn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, my starting point starts prior to 20.09 because the X-ray was done at 20.09, there was a lot of air in it by that time, so the air didn't get there at 20.08, you know, it must have been there for, you know, maybe hours, I don't know.

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Oh yes, yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: No, and to be honest in a baby that's unstable, you would not want to be -- and a baby that was paralysed, you wouldn't want to be messing about with an endotracheal tube unless you were very sure that it was in the wrong place, you would just leave well alone.

blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, it's quite difficult actually to ascertain from the notes and I have written in my report that the results were not back until 12.30. blocks.text: All right. You record next the ventilator settings.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby P]'s heart rate at 153 per minute.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Is that within the normal range?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, that's upper limit of the normal range, 153, but it's still within the normal range.

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: It wasn't a normal gas but it was certainly much, much better than the previous gas. And on this gas at 12.28 the pH is normal. The CO2 is low, but I think that is a result of the amount of ventilation he was on, but he still has a metabolic acidosis. His base excess is minus 15.4, whereas previously it had been minus 15.8.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So the base excess is the same. So it's not normal but it's certainly much better than it had been earlier on.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: The one that happened when [Dr B] and [Dr A] were in the tea room, according to the evidence of [Dr B].
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I haven't forgotten about the adrenaline infusion.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: We'll come back to that. But did further treatment follow, including the administration of inotropes?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, dobutamine was started just after 1 o'clock.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And then blood gases were being taken periodically, showing what you have described as a profound metabolic acidosis?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, the subsequent gases showed a profound metabolic acidosis with a large base excess and also a high lactate.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And in language that I can understand, what does that mean?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: It's pretty awful, to be honest. It shows a deteriorating picture because by this stage, we've had several cardiorespiratory collapses that have required large doses of adrenaline. The return of spontaneous circulation has occurred reasonably swiftly, although with each event things seem to take slightly longer and require more in terms of resuscitation drugs and fluids.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You know, they've set up a bicarbonate infusion, which is quite an unusual thing to do, they've given dopamine as an inotrope to help the heart. But despite all of that, we have still got an ongoing metabolic acidosis.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So they don't know what caused this, but they've not entirely got on top of the problem either.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Did you say dopamine or --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's interesting actually. At 13.10 dobutamine was started, but in [Dr B]'s evidence and on the fluid chart, dopamine, which is yet another inotrope, was started early on but there's no prescription for that drug in the notes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: All right. What is the point of dobutamine and dopamine in the context of a child presenting as [Baby P] was?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: These are drugs used to help the heart. Those two drugs work in slightly different ways but the end result -- the reason you give them is to try to help the heart pump better to improve the baby's blood pressure and to improve tissue perfusion so that oxygen that's being given by the ventilator can be distributed to the tissues. So after cardiorespiratory arrest, the heart usually doesn't pump that well and so these drugs increase the pumping of the heart to distribute blood and therefore oxygen around the body.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Following the administration of those drugs, were [Baby P]'s saturations restored to optimal levels?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. His saturations were 100%, you can't get any better than that. He was still on the ventilator but he was only in a
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: very small amount of oxygen by then, so he was only in 25-30% oxygen, so a very small amount.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Do we have, again, a situation in which there's been a profound respiratory collapse, but followed by an apparently successful resuscitation?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, and by then moderate ventilator settings.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: We then know that there is a watershed time, in a sense, of about 3 pm when Dr Rackham appeared. blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Again, it's not clear from the notes but what we do know is that there was a thoracocentesis, there appears to be a chest drain on this second untimed X-ray that we've seen, and finally a formal pigtail drain inserted by [Dr A] at around 15.00.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes. Just to keep the chronology, the second drain to which you have just referred is the timings taken from [Dr A]'s notes as 12.30?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I'm looking at your paragraph 3.47. Did [Baby P] enter his final and fatal cardiorespiratory arrest at about 15.40?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Was he given further doses of adrenaline, atropine, phenobarbitone, bicarbonate and other fluids?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And despite full and prolonged efforts, were those efforts or was that treatment unsuccessful?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, it was.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You then move on to give us your opinion, but before we do that, I'd like to deal with the issue that arose overtly yesterday with Dr Rackham, and it was the amount of adrenaline that was being given to [Baby P].
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: My Lord, hopefully to assist the jury following what may have been a slightly complicated explanation, we've got a further document for them with an outline explanation written, which Dr
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Bohin will supplement, which is done with the agreement and cooperation of my learned friend.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Well, you'll remember Dr Rackham saying he couldn't do the mathematics mentally in relation to this and it was going to be looked at. It has been looked at and there is essentially, as I understand it, a consensus in relation to this.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes. I'll deal with the way it's put in a moment, but yes. In fact, if it doesn't steal the prosecution's thunder, the mathematics are correct, lest that bit pass us by so (overspeaking) relieved to hear that. But we take it from there and we'll go through it in the evidence now.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: If I may say this, it's entirely for you, but don't be too worried when you look at the writing in red and how the figures are calculated. The point is, it's the consequences of the figures that are important.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I hope I'm not speaking out of turn, but there's no issue in relation to that?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Let's deal with this prescription chart. In due course, ladies and gentlemen, we'll ask you to put this behind divider 21, but it may be that for now it's best kept as a separate document.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Dr Bohin, in the bottom half of the page is there a copy of the prescription chart, which has been taken from the hospital notes?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: We can see that it appears to have been splattered with some sort of liquid.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: That's as it was received. In the bottom right-hand corner has been superimposed a red J number, 23919.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So wasn't on the original, that's a prosecution artefact, if you like. It's just the page number in the papers of the case as a whole.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I'm just going to ask you to talk us just through what we see, without any explanation first of all, what we can actually see on the green prescription form first of all.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Okay. In the top left-hand corner are the identifying features that this is a neonatal variable infusion prescription chart and it's got [Baby P]'s name, date of birth and unit number on it. Moving across that top line, it has [Baby P]'s weight of just over 2 kilograms. So for the purposes of drug calculations 2 kilograms would be used.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Below that, it says "adrenaline", and then underneath "double". And if we need to speak about that we can do.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: But adrenaline is a drug that is another inotrope drug. It can be given in other circumstances but for the purposes of this, I understand from listening to [Dr B], that they were using it as an additional drug to try and help pump the heart.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So the drug is adrenaline. The drug quantity written up is 3 milligrams. That would be a very small volume of drug and so that needs to be diluted in a compatible fluid. In this case, that dilutant is sodium chloride or normal saline.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Moving across, the final volume is 50ml. So whatever 3 milligrams of adrenaline comes to, that is added -- that will be a very small amount -- that is added to sodium chloride, so that the total volume is 50ml.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Moving across, the route is intravenous. Moving across again, the starting rate, ie the amount that you give per hour is 2ml per hour. It's then signed by -- I think it's Jessica Burke, who was the SHO, and dated the 24th.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: But if we go back across the page to where it says "adrenaline double", below the drug quantity of 3 milligrams it says in a very small box there:
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: "The final concentration of infusion."
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And that says:
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: "50 micrograms per millilitre."
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So that's the --
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Does it say 60?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Sorry, 60 micrograms per millilitre. So that's the final concentration of drug after you've added 3 milligrams of adrenaline to 50ml of normal saline.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Right. Let's just halt there and go to the --
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, it's quite complicated.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Let's go to the red text at the top. The 3 milligrams of adrenaline, which is red figure 1, so we have superimposed a red number 1 --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: -- in that box that says 3 milligrams of adrenaline.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Because the drug is to the left, adrenaline. That is equal to 3,000 micrograms, there being 1,000 micrograms in 1 milligram?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So in order to do the arithmetic, you need to reduce it to or increase it to micrograms, is that right, or alter it?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. It makes it easier, I think, for the jury to understand. Although it looks complicated it does it make it easier.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: All right. So although the form itself says 3 milligrams were put into 50 millilitres, that's 3,000 micrograms --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: -- put into 50ml of saline?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Which is figure 2, 50ml?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: That equals 60 micrograms of adrenaline per millilitre of solution?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And just to remind us of how that's worked out, that's the 3,000 milligrams of adrenaline divided by 50?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct. And that's number 4, red number 4 on your sheet.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Exactly, yes. Then we come to what you pointed out as — well, we haven't got yet to figure 3. If we're looking at the administration prescription, we have two separate orders, in effect, from Dr Burke.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: The first timed at 11.30 on the 24th?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: The rate of administration, 2ml per hour?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Of this solution that is 60 --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Micrograms per millilitre.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So that's figure 3; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So going back to the red text at the top, the third paragraph, the solution was then run at 2ml per hour, giving an overall administration rate of 120 micrograms per hour; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. So the fluids were running at 2ml an hour but that doesn't actually tell you how much drug the baby was getting per hour. So by doing a simple calculation you can see that 2ml an hour, because 1ml is 60 micrograms, 2ml an hour would be 120 micrograms per hour of adrenaline.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Thank you. We then have to work out how much that is for a particular person; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. Neonatal drugs, unlike adult drugs, are not standard there's not a standard dose for everybody. So in paediatrics and neonates, drugs are always recorded as per kilogram of body weight. So for any dose of drug you want to give, you need to work out what that means per kilogram of body weight.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Is that where we get, in effect, the fourth paragraph of red text, which is because [Baby P] weighed 2 kilograms, he was receiving 60 micrograms per kilogram per hour?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. He was having 2ml per hour, which we've just said was 120 micrograms, but he weighed 2 kilograms. So if you wanted to find out how much that drug was per kilogram, you divide it by his weight, which would give you 60.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes. So far, so good. What was the intended dose?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, unfortunately, it gets a bit more complicated than that. As well as giving drugs per kilogram per hour, some drugs are by convention noted as per kilogram per minute. So up until now, we have got to 60 micrograms per kilogram per hour, but this particular drug is prescribed and the notation -- the traditional notation is per minute, so we need to convert micrograms per kilogram per hour into micrograms per kilogram per minute.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Is this where the intended result is departed from because it's at this point of the calculation that a mistake was made?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So let's deal with that, please.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, in order to get from 60 micrograms per kilogram per hour to micrograms per kilogram per minute, given that there are 60 minutes in an hour, you divide 60 by 60 and the answer is 1 microgram per kilogram per minute.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: But what is written at item 5 is 0.5 micrograms per kilogram per minute. So that is the error.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So the intention of the prescriber, if the intention is accurately represented by the dose, which is at figure 5 on the green form, was to give 0.5 micrograms per kilogram per minute; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's what this prescriber has written that he or she would like the starting dose to be, 0.5 micrograms per kilogram per minute.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: But the result, the actual result of administering this particular fluid at the rate it was administered, was precisely double what the avowed intention was?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Right. So far, so good. We've reviewed, as we've gone through, the administration of various inotropes, which are designed, you have told us, to increase the heart rate?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And increase -- there's another word, which was used yesterday by at least one medical practitioner, was it contractility?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, that just means a squeeze of the heart.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: The power of the squeeze?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And designed also to increase blood pressure?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And that is one of the consequences of dobutamine?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, that's why you give all of the inotropes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: It's also a consequence of giving adrenaline, or it may be?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's what you're hoping for, yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes. In the context of our everyday lives, we're all wittingly or unwittingly familiar with the administration of adrenaline, aren't we, generally speaking?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Maybe more in the witness box than in his Lordship's chair sometimes?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: What is adrenaline?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Adrenaline is a naturally occurring hormone produced by a gland that sits just above the kidneys. It's produced at times of stress, hence your indication about it may be high if you're in the witness box. It's produced at times when you have a fight-or-flight response. So in stressful situations the body automatically makes you ready for some impending attack or to deal with something stressful. So at that time everyone will be familiar with their heart pounding in their chest and that is the response of adrenaline.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So we all have experience of it to that degree at least.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Now, what effect did this apparent overdose of adrenaline have in this case?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I don't think it had any -- well, it didn't have any adverse effect in that it was -- the infusion was started after [Baby P] had had at least two of his collapses and already had a metabolic acidosis by then, as we've already established. Looking at what happened after the adrenaline was started, albeit at double the dose that was intended by this prescriber, his blood pressure -- it didn't really have any effect on his blood pressure, his blood pressure didn't go up. That is a potential consequence, that you'll get a sudden rise in blood pressure, which in premature babies can be a problem.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: This didn't happen.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: It can also cause the heart rate to go up very briskly; that also didn't happen. And it can also cause lactic acidosis. But of course, [Baby P] already had a lactic acidosis. So it's difficult -- it's impossible for me to estimate what contribution this dose of adrenaline made to the lactic acidosis, but it certainly didn't effect his blood pressure or his heart rate adversely.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: They were trying to raise it and it didn't have that effect in the end, did it?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No, and by this time he was on three inotropes, which in premature neonates is extremely, extremely unusual.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Going back to the position immediately following [Baby P]'s premature death then, please, Dr Bohin. What conclusions did you draw from all the evidence as we have summarised it to be?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Firstly, I was concerned about the initial abdominal Xray taken and the amount of gas within that X-ray because that X-ray was taken as almost a precautionary measure by Dr Gibbs at a time when there was no actual clinical concern about [Baby P]'s abdomen. Yet we can see on the X-ray that the abdomen is full of gas. Dr Arthurs described it as moderately full of gas, but there's gas that goes from the stomach and there's abdominal distension right the way through the bowel to the rectum.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: That's tile 173. So that's the 20.09 --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's the 20.09 X-ray.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: -- X-ray on 23 June?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: The night before.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I'm sorry, could you take up where I so rudely interrupted?

blocks.text: Right. Well, let's see. But is that not a link you were making? We'll come to your report in a moment.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I was making the link with abdominal distension with the collapse at 9.40. The abdominal X-ray was abnormal.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I made the link with abdominal distension because it was noted by the nurse looking after him that morning and he had had episodes of being intolerant of feed overnight.

blocks.text: "Prior to his collapse, [Baby P] had a very abnormal gas pattern on his abdominal X-ray on 23 June."

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: You say that?

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's where you get to on the conclusion, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: And I'm suggesting, first of all, you're drawing a link from where you say from the exogenous gas injected into the bowel seen in the gas pattern and gastric dilation splinting the diaphragm. That's what you're doing in the report, isn't it?

blocks.text: No. There is an abnormal gas pattern and I think that exogenous air is responsible for that.

blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So we can be clear what it says in the conclusion, the wording, I'm going to suggest, matters, you say:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "The abnormal gas pattern is the result of exogenous gas injected into the bowel."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And you then say:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "The collapse is most likely to have occurred as a result of the gastric dilation splinting the diaphragm."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: When you say "the gastric dilation", that refers to the exogenous gas into the bowel, doesn't it?

blocks.text: No. It's poor wording on my part, so I'm sorry, I apologise.

blocks.text: No.

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: splinting being caused by gas the night before; do you disagree with that?

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "NG tube on free drainage. Trace amount in tube. Abdomen full. Loops visible, soft to touch."

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: And there's reference to abdomen distended when Dr Ukoh is there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: It can be. It's not diagnostic, but it doesn't exclude it.

blocks.text: "Abdo full but soft."

blocks.text: Do you see that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Abdo full, slightly loopy."

blocks.text: In fact we know later that day, as it happens, [Baby O] collapsed. But I'm suggesting to you an abdomen full and slightly loopy, for whatever reason, is something that can occur in a baby quite naturally.

blocks.text: Yes, it may occur, but you can't look at it in isolation, you have to put it into the context of what else has happened. blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: We're dealing with [Baby P] now, 24 June. That's at tile 289, the second page. We have the reported matters first and then on the next page we have what he found which includes:

blocks.text: "On examination: mildly pale, no recession, and abdomen moderately distended and bloated, skin slightly mottled."

blocks.text: Do you see that?

blocks.text: Yes, soft abdomen, yes.

blocks.text: But certainly no indication at that point of a baby whose diaphragm has been splinted by excessive air, is there?

blocks.text: Not at that point, but 10 minutes later he has a cardiac arrest.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Well, something happens, undoubtedly.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Because he's got a distended abdomen and there obviously becomes a tipping point where the baby will tolerate having abdominal distension for a certain amount of time, but then is unable to tolerate it because the diaphragm becomes splinted by the gaseous distension and the baby decompensates.

blocks.text: We have heard from Dr Ukoh. Nothing in his examination indicated, we are told, anything like the collapse that was going to follow -- was it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, it was completely unexpected and unexplained.

blocks.text: And the abdomen is described simply as "distended moderately", isn't it?

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: Do you see that?

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: I know we've heard about this before, but some of us may not remember the full details of what pulmonary hypertension is first of all. So in a few sentences, could you just explain the concept of pulmonary hypertension?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Pulmonary hypertension, particularly in babies, is where there's an increased pressure of blood flow to the lungs, and it can affect the blood flow within the heart, it can affect oxygenation -- subsequent oxygenation and blood pressure. In newborn babies it's an attempt for them to try to revert to the
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: condition that they were when they were inside their mum's tummy, but of course you don't want them to revert to that condition. And if they develop pulmonary hypertension there is difficulty in oxygenating those babies because of the high blood pressures in the lungs.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Does it stop the oxygen going out in the arteries round the body in effect?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: In a simplistic way of dealing with it, yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Simple is better for me!
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I think -- yes, without getting into detailed physiology, it means that that high pressure inhibits oxygenation so the babies have low saturations and ultimately a low heart rate and you have to put in quite -- it's a very difficult thing to treat, so you do your best to prevent it happening. And if it does develop, you have to put very specific strategies in place to try and treat it, to overcome it and reverse that action.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: In the context of a child who might have in their differential diagnosis pulmonary hypertension as a possibility, if a child may have pulmonary hypertension, would it actually be an advantage to treating them to have a high general blood pressure?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That is one of the treatments, that -- and I think Dr Rackham said yesterday as well that one of the things he was considering was pulmonary hypertension and if you think a child may be developing that, one of the ways of treating it is to make sure that the blood pressure in the body, as opposed to in the lungs, is higher than -- you would set it higher than you normally would using inotropes. There's a variety of inotropes you can use but actually adrenaline is in certain -- in the North-west Neonatal Unit Team, adrenaline is the drug -- is the inotrope of choice to try and prevent pulmonary hypertension because one of the side effects, potential side effects, is that actually it reduces the blood flow to the lungs paradoxically.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN
